new_statements.quote: Kinubi presents a reduced five-vowels system (a, e, i, o, u); as in Turku and Juba Arabic, stress is lexically distinctive as in the opposition between sába "seven" and sabá "morning" (Owens 1985: 145).
new_statements.citation: Tosco, Mauro & Stefano Manfredi. 2013. Pidgins and creoles. In Jonathan Owens (ed.), The Oxford Handbook of Arabic Linguistics, 495-519. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
new_statements.locator: p. 504, section 22.4.2 Kinubi (phonology paragraph); cf. p. 502 section 22.4.1 Turku and Bongor Arabic
new_statements.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
new_statements.rule_in_words: The handbook chapter states in passing that Turku, like Juba Arabic and Kinubi, has lexically distinctive (contrastive) stress; the minimal pair given (saba 'seven' vs saba 'morning') is Kinubi, not Turku, and no Turku stress rule or Turku minimal pair is given. The same chapter's Turku paragraph (p. 502) says only that Turku 'presents a reduced phonology in which secondary consonant realizations and long vowels are absent'. Avram 2020 (open, on file) adds for Turku that vowel length is not distinctive but says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the claim about Turku is a one-clause aside inside the Kinubi section.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical contrast). The source is a survey chapter; the primary description it rests on, Tosco & Owens 1993 (Tosco is co-author of both), was not opened. Muraz 1926, the only data source for Turku (French colonial orthography), may not mark stress at all, so the basis of the Turku claim is unverified here.
new_statements.identity_note: Target is the extinct pidgin Turku (Tourkou) of the Chari-Baguirmi region, Chad, known only from Muraz 1926; Glottolog 5.3 names it 'Turku-Bongor Pidgin Arabic' and lists the living Bongor Pidgin Arabic (bong1302, Mayo-Kebbi Est, Luffin 2007/2013) as a dialect under turk1244. The quoted statement concerns Turku proper; Luffin's Bongor Arabic material (with stress-marked transcriptions) would apply to the dialect bong1302.

sources.note: Read via web lookups: lexicon and calques only, no phonology or stress. Introduction states Muraz (1926) has a grammatical sketch pp. 11-17, ~1,300-entry vocabulary pp. 113-187, six dialogues pp. 265-294, and that 'the phonology, morphology and syntax of Turku are analyzed in detail by Tosco & Owens (1993)'.
Turku Arabic: no phonology. Bongor Arabic (citing Luffin 2013: 162): long vowels became 'short stressed vowels'; nothing on stress placement.
